overview: The A:shiwi, or Zuni, are a living Pueblo people with ancestral settlements in western New Mexico. Hawikku was one of several major communities. The map’s 1530 to 1650 interval captures part of the colonial encounter; it does not define Zuni society’s lifetime.

periods.title: Ancestral towns
periods.summary: Archaeology at Hawikku reveals a large pueblo occupied before Spanish arrival.

periods.title: Invasion and missions
periods.summary: Spanish conquest and missionary demands brought conflict to Zuni settlements.

periods.title: Resistance and continuing communities
periods.summary: The Pueblo Revolt changed colonial rule; Zuni people and institutions endured.

sections.title: Homes and objects from ancestral towns

items.text: At Hawikku, archaeologists identified six large building groups separated by passages and small plazas. Parts rose one to three stories. Such a pueblo required coordinated building and shared circulation space, while its households lived close enough to hear plenty of their neighbors’ daily activity.

Hawikku’s builders bound local sandstone with adobe mortar or red clay, then smoothed walls with plaster. Rooms and foundations survive alongside unexcavated areas, preserving this careful combination of stone masonry and earthen finishing.

A jar excavated in 1920 from Room 172 of Hawikku’s House Group F is dated 1630 to 1680 by the Smithsonian. It was built by coiling clay, then painted and glazed. Its recorded room context and probable A:shiwi attribution make it a specific witness to craft during the colonial period.

Coronado’s forces attacked and occupied Hawikku in 1540. A mission was established there in 1629, bringing new religious demands and tensions. The pueblo’s substantial buildings existed before these arrivals; Spanish hopes of finding cities of gold tell us about the invaders’ expectations, not Zuni priorities.

In 1680, A:shiwi communities joined the Pueblo Revolt against Spanish colonizers and the mission at Halona was burned. The Zuni Tribal Archives records its later reestablishment around 1700. Resistance and rebuilding changed the use of familiar places while Zuni communities continued.

sections.title: Gardens that hold on to water

items.text: A photograph catalogued to about 1912 shows women planting Zuni waffle gardens. Small square depressions held water carried from the river in buckets. Their name describes the garden’s patterned surface; breakfast waffles were not growing in the soil.

In its 2021 gardening program, the Zuni Youth Enrichment Project enrolled 100 families and distributed 88 rain barrels; 12 families requested gutter kits. Catching roof runoff brought another water source to home gardens. The practical goal was to keep useful rain from simply running away.

The local utility partnered with the youth project on rain collection and water-bill rebates. Garden irrigation could then use stored rain while conserving the municipal supply for households. Water management linked children’s activities, family gardening and public infrastructure.

The youth project’s food programs began with lessons in traditional waffle gardens led by local agriculture leaders. Its later activities include young interns teaching younger children and school classes preparing meals. Growing and cooking food become ways for different generations to learn together.

For the Hawikku exhibition opened in 2002, Zuni representatives selected 221 objects from the Smithsonian collection. Displaying these ancestral materials in the community connects archaeological finds with descendants’ own accounts. It also invites discussion of the earlier excavations, which the museum explicitly describes as controversial.

The museum’s map-art exhibition brings together 31 paintings by 16 Zuni artists. These works record migration histories, ancestral places, water, plants and other relationships. A map can express remembered connections and cultural meaning as well as distances and boundary lines.

The tribal newsletter reported a 2022 film of the Zuni Turkey Maiden story, developed through a community oral-history project. Earlier recordings of elders from the 1960s helped inspire new performances. Film and online viewing carried a long tradition into a different medium, within community storytelling protocols.

Writing sample: “Elahkwa” means “Thank you,” as printed with its translation on the A:shiwi A:wan Museum’s contact page. This is contemporary community writing in the Latin alphabet. It represents the living Zuni language, rather than a reconstructed inscription from Hawikku.

ending.text: Zuni people did not disappear when particular ancestral pueblos were abandoned or when colonial rule changed. Their community preserves and interprets those places, teaches language and maintains its own governing institutions. The map’s 1650 cutoff is only a coverage limit; the Pueblo of Zuni continues today.
